item.title: How I Do It: An Intensivist's guide to RV Failure and Right Ventricular Assist Devices
item.description:
Right ventricular failure (RVF) is a high-mortality form of cardiogenic shock frequently encountered in critical illness and is often underrecognized due to its heterogeneous presentation. This article presents a physiology-driven, stepwise approach to the diagnosis and management of acute RVF using a longitudinal case in the intensive care unit. We highlight practical bedside tools for recognition, including point-of-care ultrasound and invasive hemodynamics, and review targeted strategies for preload optimization, afterload reduction, and contractility support. Special emphasis is placed on airway management, vasoactive medications, and timely escalation to mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in appropriately selected patients. This bedside "How I Do It" guide is written for intensivists and pulmonary/critical care clinicians and translates advanced hemodynamic and device concepts into practical decision points for acute care management.

Sridhar M, Patel M, Manek G, Chowdhury J, Villalobos N, Soto F

item.title: Comparative Effectiveness of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists versus DPP-4 and SGLT2 Inhibitors in Patients with Bronchiectasis and Type 2 Diabetes
item.description:
Background: Bronchiectasis is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with limited disease-modifying therapies. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, but their impact on bronchiectasis outcomes remains unknown.

Research question: Is GLP-1RA use, compared with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i) or sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) use, associated with better clinical outcomes in patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes (T2D)?

Study design and methods: Using the TriNetX global federated research network, we conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes who initiated GLP-1RA therapy between June 1, 2022, and May 30, 2025. We compared clinical outcomes, including all-cause mortality, bronchiectasis exacerbation, acute respiratory failure, and lower respiratory tract infections, with patients receiving DPP-4i) or SGLT2i using propensity score matching to balance baseline characteristics.

Results: After propensity score matching, 1,029 patients per group were included in the GLP-1RA versus DPP-4i cohort, and 2,255 patients per group in the GLP-1RA versus SGLT2i cohort. Compared with DPP-4i, GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (hazard ratio [HR], 0.43; 95% CI, 0.33-0.56) and reduced risks of acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.36-0.58) and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.46-0.65). Similar benefits were observed compared with SGLT2i for all-cause mortality (HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.40-0.60), acute respiratory failure (HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.39-0.55), and lower respiratory tract infection (HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.68-0.86). Stratified analyses demonstrated consistent mortality benefits across demographic and clinical subgroups, with particularly pronounced effects in obese patients but there was no statistically significant reduction in bronchiectasis exacerbations.

Interpretation: Among patients with bronchiectasis and type 2 diabetes, GLP-1RA therapy was associated with significantly lower mortality and reduced respiratory complications compared with DPP-4i or SGLT2i. These findings suggest potential disease-modifying benefits of GLP-1RAs in bronchiectasis beyond glycemic control.

item.title: The Burden of Chronic Cough in Patients With Interstitial Lung Disease: a US Survey-Based Analysis of Its Effects on Daily Life and Emotional and Social Well-Being
item.description:
Background: Chronic cough (≥8 weeks) is highly prevalent among patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and non-IPF interstitial lung disease (ILD) and imposes significant physical, social, and psychological burden. Research characterizing the burden of chronic cough in patients with IPF and non-IPF ILD from the patient perspective is limited.

Research question: What is the multidimensional burden of chronic cough in patients living with IPF or non-IPF ILD?

Study design and methods: An online cross-sectional survey was distributed to adults from June to July 2025 via the Pulmonary Fibrosis Foundation's US Community Registry. Eligibility required a self-reported diagnosis of IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough. Multiple-choice and open-text questions spanned six domains: demographics, disease history, cough characteristics, daily life impact, social/emotional and long-term impact, and healthcare experience.

Results: A total of 197 participants completed the survey: 75.63% reported a diagnosis of IPF, 21.32% reported non-IPF ILD, and 3.05% were awaiting further ILD diagnosis. Participants reported cough-related interference with daily activities (76.15%) and sleep disruption (79.69%) within the preceding week. Emotional burden was frequently reported: 95.94% of participants had cough-induced worry, 75.13% had depression, sadness, or low mood, and 67.01% reported avoiding social situations because of cough. Additionally, 60.91% of participants reported that chronic cough affected their platonic relationships, and 55.33% reported impact on their ability or desire to maintain physical or intimate relationships. To treat cough, participants reported using an average of 2.7 therapeutic classes historically and 2.0 classes currently, with many reporting limited or no relief.

Interpretation: Findings from this US survey of patients with IPF or non-IPF ILD and chronic cough indicate that, among respondents, chronic cough burden manifests physically, psychologically, and psychosocially. Reports of limited relief from available therapies suggest an unmet need in managing chronic cough in this patient population.

Clinical trial registration: Not applicable.

item.title: Pragmatic Clinical indicators of Tuberculosis Transmission Risk: a Household Contact Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: Interrupting TB transmission is a priority in high-burden settings. Identifying highly infectious people with TB may guide targeted interventions.

Research question: Can readily available clinical characteristics (eg, lung cavitation, cough duration, modified Bandim TB score) indicate the transmission risk in participants with TB?

Study design and methods: We conducted an observational cohort study in Lima, Peru, enrolling 4,500 index participants. Of the 4,044 people with microbiologically confirmed TB, 3,109 had at least 1 household contact (HHC), yielding 12,767 HHCs. Index participants underwent chest radiograph and TB symptom assessment, from which we derived a modified Bandim TB score. We assessed HHCs for TB infection at baseline and 6 months, and for incident TB disease over 12 months. We analyzed associations between index participant indicators and TB outcomes in HHCs using modified Poisson regression with generalized estimating equations, adjusting for relevant covariates.

Results: Among child HHCs, baseline TB infection risk increased with greater cavitary extent (adjusted trend P = .005) and longer cough duration (adjusted trend P = .002), with similar trends at 6 months. Among cavitation categories, multiple-quadrant involvement was associated with the highest baseline infection risk (adjusted prevalence risk ratio, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.10-2.39), but not with incident disease (adjusted cumulative risk ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 0.56-2.60). Among cough duration categories, ≥ 56 days showed the highest baseline infection risk (adjusted prevalence risk ratio, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.18-2.13), but not incident disease (adjusted cumulative risk ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 0.85-1.99). The modified Bandim TB score was not associated with transmission risk.

Interpretation: Our results show that in this large household cohort, cavitary extent on chest radiograph and cough duration in people with TB were associated with increased TB transmission risk and showed dose-response relationships with TB infection. These simple, readily available indicators may help target preventive interventions in high-burden settings; however, associations with incident TB remain uncertain.

item.title: Associations between temperatures, extreme temperature events, and onset of acute exacerbations of COPD: a time-stratified case-crossover study in China
item.description:
Background: Non-optimal temperatures and extreme temperature events may trigger acute exacerbations of COPD (AECOPD), but most evidence is admission based, potentially misclassifying exposure timing and obscuring susceptible groups.

Research question: Are non-optimal temperature and extreme temperature events associated with AECOPD onset, and which patients are most susceptible?

Study design and methods: We used the Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Registry (ACURE) data and assigned residential temperature exposure using ERA5-Land, a reanalysis dataset of European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Cold spells (CS) were defined as consecutive days below location-specific low-temperature thresholds, and compound cold spells (CCS) as concurrent daytime and nighttime cold spells. Associations with reported symptom onset were estimated using a time-stratified case-crossover design, conditional logistic regression with distributed lag nonlinear models. Subgroup and cytokine analyses assessed susceptibility and inflammation.

Results: Among 5,634 patients with AECOPD (mean age, 69.4 ± 9.5 years; 78.8% male), lower temperature was associated with higher odds of AECOPD onset, whereas higher temperature was not. The strongest associations occurred for CS lasting ≥3 days and CCS lasting ≥2 days over lag 0-3 days, with ORs of 1.84 (95% CI, 1.22-2.78) and 4.31 (95% CI, 2.07-8.97), respectively. Nearly half had delayed admission within 14 days. Using admission rather than onset dates attenuated estimates by 88.8% for CS and 84.8% for CCS. Associations were stronger among older adults, men, smokers, patients with severe AECOPD in the past year or previously diagnosed COPD, and those using combination inhaler in the preceding year. CS were also associated with higher TNF-α, IL-6, and CXCL-11 concentrations.

Interpretation: Lower temperature and extreme cold events, particularly CCS, were associated with AECOPD onset. Symptom-onset timing may better capture temperature-related associations than admission timing. These findings highlight the need for targeted cold-weather prevention strategies to reduce AECOPD burden.

item.title: Mediastinal Mass With Recurrent Hemorrhagic Pleural Effusion
item.description:
A 55-year-old man was admitted with a 2-year history of recurrent dyspnea and exertional breathlessness, accompanied by intermittent blood-tinged sputum. During this period, he had been hospitalized 7 times at external institutions, where he underwent extensive investigations including fiberoptic bronchoscopy, endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration, mediastinoscopy, thoracoscopy, and CT imaging-guided biopsy of a mediastinal mass. Empirical antituberculosis therapy also was administered, but no definitive diagnosis was established.

item.title: A 63-Year-Old Man With Dyspnea and Loculated Pleural Effusion
item.description:
A 63-year-old man with a past medical history of hypertension and end-stage renal disease receiving scheduled hemodialysis via a left upper extremity fistula sought treatment for shortness of breath of 1 to 2 years' duration that worsened acutely for 1 day after missing a hemodialysis session. In addition, the patient reported mild central chest pain without radiation. He otherwise was in his usual state of health and did not report fevers, chills, cough, sputum production, wheezing, abdominal pain, or hemoptysis. He reported history of tobacco use, having smoked one-half a pack of cigarettes for 15 years and quit about 15 years ago.

item.title: Persistent Severe OSA Despite Ongoing CPAP Therapy
item.description:
A 51-year-old man was referred to our sleep medicine clinic for reevaluation of previously diagnosed OSA. The diagnosis had been established approximately 4 years earlier, at a body weight of 105 kg (BMI, 31.7 kg/m2). At that time, cardiorespiratory polygraphy documented severe OSA, with an apnea-hypopnea index of 97 events/h. Mean nocturnal oxygen saturation (Spo2) was 91%, and the cumulative time spent with Spo2 < 90% accounted for 38% of the total recording time, indicating a substantial nocturnal hypoxemic burden. Nocturnal CPAP therapy had been prescribed, delivered through an oronasal mask at a fixed pressure of 11 cm H2O.

item.title: Bilateral Pulmonary Nodules After Lung Transplantation: A Rare Diagnosis
item.description:
A 64-year-old man who underwent bilateral orthotopic lung transplant for emphysema related to α1-antitrypsin deficiency 8 months ago presented to the clinic for assessment of bilateral pulmonary nodules identified on routine postlung transplant surveillance without any symptomatic concerns. The donor was positive for cytomegalovirus and positive for Epstein-Barr virus, and the recipient was negative for cytomegalovirus and positive for Epstein-Barr virus. He denied any fever, chills, cough, chest pain, dyspnea, weight loss, or night sweats. The patient lived in South Florida with no recent travel history outside the United States or infectious contacts. His posttransplant course was complicated with antibody-mediated rejection at 1.5 months after lung transplant. Antibody-mediated rejection was successfully treated with our institutional multimodal regimen, including a combination of plasmapheresis, carfilzomib, and anti-thymocyte globulin followed by monthly IV immunoglobulin and tocilizumab injections. Also, because of calcineurin inhibitor (CNI)-related renal dysfunction, the patient's immunosuppression was converted to a belatacept-based CNI-sparing regimen in addition to prednisone, with a tacrolimus goal trough of 4 to 6 ng/mL. He was also placed on mycophenolic acid, which was soon held because of neutropenia.

item.title: A Young Man With Hypereosinophilia and Pseudochylothorax
item.description:
A 31-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of dry cough, progressive dyspnea, intermittent fever, and unintentional weight loss of 8 kg. He had no wheezing, hemoptysis, chest pain, palpitations, or skin rashes. He did not smoke and reported occasional alcohol intake. One year earlier, he had been diagnosed elsewhere with pleuro-pericardial TB based on an ultrasound showing right-sided pleural effusion, and 2-dimensional echocardiography showed pericardial effusion. Pleural fluid analysis showed a lymphocytic exudative pleural effusion with elevated adenosine deaminase levels (46 IU/mL). The patient received anti-tubercular therapy along with tapering corticosteroids, showing initial clinical improvement. He was employed as a soldier in the army, and his last posting was in northeast India, where he frequently consumed raw crabs pickled in alcohol. There was no other significant environmental history.
